four.etymology: From Latin foris, foras. Compare Italian fuori, Friulian fûr, Dalmatian fure, Venetan fora.

aria.etymology: Inherited from Latin āera, Greek-type accusative of āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”).

non.etymology: From Latin nōmen. Compare Friulian non, Dalmatian naun.

me.etymology: From Latin mē, accusative singular of ego.

cor.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n.

la.etymology: From Latin illa(m), feminine of ille.

aqua.etymology: From Latin aqua from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ékʷeh₂. Compare Venetan àcua, Italian acqua.

arma.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms, weapons of war, war, defense, tools”).

pera.etymology: From Latin petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra).

amen.etymology: Borrowed from Latin āmēn, from Ancient Greek ἀμήν (amḗn), from Biblical Hebrew אָמֵן (ʾāmēn, “certainly, truly”).

gila.etymology: From Latin illa, feminine of ille. Compare Piedmontese chila, Dalmatian jala.

anda.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin andāre.

banca.etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic bank, from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz.

alto.etymology: From Latin altus (“high”), from Proto-Italic *altos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eltós, derived from the root *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”).

alba.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *alba, from Latin albus (“white”).

mel.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n.

bianco.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin blancus, from Frankish *blank. Compare Italian bianco, Dalmatian blanc.

bro.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin brodium, from Frankish *broþ, from Proto-Germanic *bruþą.

pais.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pagenses, from Late Latin pāgēnsis (“inhabitant of a district”), from Latin pāgus (“village; district”). Compare Italian paese, Venetan pajès, Friulian paîs, Sicilian paisi, Romansh pajais, Catalan país, French pays, Port

spada.etymology: From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē).

*Borrowed from Ligurian boa, from Lombardic *bauga.

core.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n. Compare Italian cuore.

puoi.etymology: From Latin post. Compare Italian poi, Venetan po, può.

agosto.etymology: From Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus.

sul.etymology: From Latin sōl. Compare Dalmatian saul, Venetan sołe, Italian sole.

banda.etymology: From Old Occitan, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *bindā (“tie, join, link”). Compare French bande, Italian banda.

barca.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin barca, probably derived from Latin baris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris).

bati.etymology: Inherited from Latin battuere, from Latin battuō.

bulo.etymology: Inherited from Medieval Latin bullāre, from Latin bulla.

anca.etymology: Possibly from Latin hanc hodie or Latin hanc quam (horam). Compare Venetan and Dalmatian anca, Italian anche, Friulian ancje.

boro.etymology: Borrowed from Venetan boro, from borro, borra (“round object”).

sento.etymology: From Latin centum; cf. Venetan sento.

bosco.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin boscus, from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

urma.etymology: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *orma or *osma, from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ). Compare Italian orma, Romanian urmă, also Spanish husma and Venetan usma.

caca.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cacca, possibly from or related to Ancient Greek κάκκη (kákkē, “dung”).

ura.etymology: From Latin hōra. Cognate with Sicilian ura.

ridi.etymology: Plural derived from Latin rēte. Compare Italian reti.

lito.etymology: From Latin lēctus, perfect passive participle of legō. Compare Italian letto.

ansi.etymology: Either from Latin antea or from Latin ante.

bastón.etymology: From Latin battuere, itself of unknown origin.

paja.etymology: From Latin palea, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”); compare Venetan paja.

biga.etymology: Either from Latin biga (“chariot”) or from a combination Venetan bina' and figa.

nui.etymology: From Latin nōs. Compare Italian noi, Sicilian nui, Dalmatian nu.

briga.etymology: Either from Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”) or from Proto-Celtic *brīgos. Cognate with Italian briga.

baro.etymology: Probably from Proto-Celtic *barros. Cognate with Welsh bar and Irish barr.

bava.etymology: For the first sense, inherited from Vulgar Latin *baba, of nursery origin. For the second one, compare Italian bava di vento.

blu.etymology: Borrowed from French bleu (“blue”) from Middle French bleu, from Old French blou, bleve (“pallid, wan, discoloured/discolored, blue”), from Frankish *blāu, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue, yellowish-gray”).

beba.etymology: Inherited from Latin pappa (“food for children”).

cào.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”).

baso.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bassus, from uncertain origin.

glosses_en: quantity of things not precisely defined, objects
broto.etymology: Possibly from Old High German borto (“ribbon”), with metathesis of /r/.

cesa.etymology: From Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía). Compare Venetan cexa, Italian chiesa.

vuoi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin voleō, from Latin volō. Compare Italian voglio.

sil.etymology: From Latin caelum. Compare Dalmatian cil.

lù.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *illūi, from Latin illī, dative singular of ille. Compare Italian lui.

zì.etymology: Inherited from Latin īre. Compare Dalmatian zer.

russo.etymology: From Latin russus. Compare Italian rosso.

sasso.etymology: Ultimately from Latin saxum. Compare Italian sasso.

braso.etymology: Inherited from Latin brāchium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn).

magnà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin mandicāre, from Latin manducāre. Cf. Venetan magnar, Italian magnare.

cume.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *quomo (from Latin quomōdo) + et. Compare Italian come, French comme, Romanian cum.

infierno.etymology: From Latin īnfernum, neuter form of īnfernus (“of the lower regions”). Compare Dalmatian infiarn.

dèi.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin diēs. Compare Dalmatian dai, Venetan and archaic Italian dì.

piova.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *plovia, from Latin pluvia. Compare Venetan pióva.

grando.etymology: From Latin grandis. Compare also Venetan grando.

brivido.etymology: Probably onomatopoeic. Cognate with Italian brivido.

bafo.etymology: Uncertain. Doria suggests etymology maybe derived from Ancient Greek βᾰφή (băphḗ). Cognate with Italian baffo, Venetan bafo.

arso.etymology: Inherited from Latin ārsus, from ārdeō.

tamur.etymology: From Latin timor, timōrem. Compare Italian timore.

curda.etymology: From Latin chorda, from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, cord”).

caval.etymology: From Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”).

duona.etymology: From Late Latin domna, shortened variant of Latin domina.

arsura.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin ārsūra, from Latin ārsus.

forsa.etymology: From Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”).

baio.etymology: Borrowed from French baille, from Late Latin baiula.

brufolo.etymology: Possibly a blend of Latin verrūcam + Latin rūfulum (“red-haired”).

sensa.etymology: Probably ultimately from Latin absentia. Compare Venetan sensa, Dalmatian siansa, Italian senza.

beco.etymology: Word of uncertain etymology: some favor borrowing from German Bock (“male goat”), or becch, a word imitating the bleating of the goat; others propose an onomatopoeic base *bek and a pre-Roman Alpine substrate reflected in the Latin ibicem (

duopo.etymology: From Latin de post. Compare Dalmatian dapú, Venetan dapò, Italian dopo, Romanian după, Sicilian dopu, Friulian daspò, French depuis.

brenta.etymology: Inherited from Latin brenta, of pre-Roman substrate origin. Used widely in Northern Italy.

ciapà.etymology: Ultimately from Late Latin capulāre (through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *clapāre, after metathesis), from Latin capulum. Cf. Venetan ciapar. Compare Italian chiappare, Friulian cjapâ, Venetan ciapar.

glosses_en: first-person singular present indicative of avì

quil.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu illu, contracted from the accusative of Vulgar Latin *eccum ille. Compare Italian quello, Venetan cuel, cuelo.

laro.etymology: From Latin latrō. Compare Venetan laro, ladro, Friulian lari, Italian ladro.

vardà.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.

frido.etymology: From Latin frīgidus (“cold, cool, chilling”) (through a syncopated Vulgar Latin form *frigdus, fricdus), from frīgeō, frīgēre (“be cold”).

omo.etymology: From Latin homō. Compare Venetan omo, Italian uomo.

passà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).

baréta.etymology: Probably borrowed from Old Italian baretta, from Late Latin birretum (“linen headgear”), diminutive of birrus (“cloak, woollen cap”).

cascà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *cāsicāre, derived from Latin cadere. Compare Italian cascare, Venetan cascar.

àmia.etymology: Inherited from Latin amita. Compare Venetan àmia, Dalmatian amia.

becarìa.etymology: From beccaio, cognate with Venetan becarìa.

the collar of a men's dress shirt
botéga.etymology: Inherited from Latin apothēca, from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”).

butiro.etymology: Inherited from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτῡρον (boútūron).

almanco.etymology: From al + manco. Cognate with Italian almanco, Catalan almanco.

ciave.etymology: Ultimately from Latin clāvis. Cf. Venetan ciave.

babo.etymology: From Serbo-Croatian baba (“grandmother”), an allusion to grandmothers.

gnanca.etymology: From anca. Compare Venetan gnanca, nianca, nanca, Italian neanche, Friulian nancje.

ciamà.etymology: Ultimately from Latin clāmāre, possibly through Venetan ciamar; compare also Italian chiamare.

tenpo.etymology: From Latin tempus. Compare Venetan tenpo, Dalmatian tianp.

glosses_en: snake (non-poisonous, such as the grass snake)
bìsa.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin bīstia, from Latin bēstia.

salvà.etymology: From Late Latin salvō (“to save”), from Latin salvus.

luri.etymology: From Latin illōrum. Compare Venetan łuri, łori, łore, Italian loro.

miera.etymology: From Latin milliāria, plural of milliārium. Compare Italian migliaia.

brága.etymology: Inherited from Latin brācae, of Transalpine Gaulish origin.

lezi.etymology: From Latin legere. Compare Venetan lèzar, lèzer, Italian leggere.

puorta.etymology: From Latin porta. Compare Dalmatian puarta, Italian porta, Friulian puarte, Romanian poartă.

Compare French bramer, Italian bramare and Spanish bramar.

veîn.etymology: From Latin vīnum. Compare Dalmatian vain.

rustèi.etymology: Of Germanic origin; cf. Frankish *rōstjan (“to roast”), from Proto-Germanic *raustijaną (“to roast”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hrews- (“to crackle, roast”). Compare Italian arrostire.

virdo.etymology: From Vulgar Latin virdis (possibly through the intermediate of Venetan vérdo), syncopated from Classical Latin viridis. Cf. Italian verde, Dalmatian viard.

taiatro.etymology: From Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”).

sugno.etymology: From Latin somnium. Compare Italian sogno.

ondaze.etymology: From Latin ūndecim. Compare Venetan undexe, ondexe, Italian undici.

fameîa.etymology: From Latin familia. Compare Venetan faméja.

cunpagno.etymology: From Late Latin compāniō (whence also Italian compagno, French copain), from cum + pānis.

pazà.etymology: From Latin pēnsāre. Doublet of pansà. Compare Venetan pexar, Italian pesare, Neapolitan penzà, Friulian pesâ, Romanian păsa.

senpro.etymology: From Latin semper or from Venetan senpro. Compare also Dalmatian sianpro, siampro.

soûcaro.etymology: From Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), probably with multiple Romance intermediaries. Compare Venetan sùcaro, Italian zucchero.

masà.etymology: Compare Venetan masar, Italian ammazzare, Friulian maçâ, Romansh mazzar, Occitan massar, cf. also Spanish mazar.

zento.etymology: From Latin gēns, gentem. Compare Venetan zente, Dalmatian ziant, Italian gente.

zalo.etymology: Ultimately from Latin galbinus, possibly through Italian giallo, itself from Old French jalne, or through Venetan xało, zało; cf. also Friulian zâl, Dalmatian zuola and, perhaps, Sicilian zallu.

zanucio.etymology: From Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”). Compare Venetan zenocio.

fanucio.etymology: From Late Latin fēnuculum (through a later contracted Vulgar Latin form *fenuclum), from a diminutive of Latin fēnum. Compare Venetan fenocio, Italian finocchio.

ciuodo.etymology: Ultimately from Latin clāvus, through a later Vulgar Latin form *claus, with the addition of a -d- due to influence from claudō. Possibly through Venetan ciodo; compare also Italian chiodo, Friulian claud.

giasso.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs. Compare Italian ghiaccio.

mas'cio.etymology: From Vulgar Latin masclus, from Latin masculus, possibly through Venetan mas-cio; compare also Italian maschio.

bies'cia.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bīstia, from Latin bēstia. Compare Italian biscia.

bas'ciamà.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre).

zugadur.etymology: From a derivative of Latin iocor. Compare Venetan xugadore, Italian giocatore, Friulian zuiadôr.

sugnadur.etymology: From a derivative of the Latin verb somniāre or from Latin somniātor. Compare Italian sognatore.

doûto.etymology: From Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Latin tōtus. Compare Italian tutto, Venetan tuto, Friulian dut.

gialìto.etymology: From Latin dialectos, from Ancient Greek διάλεκτος (diálektos).

giamanto.etymology: From Late Latin diamas, diamantis, from Latin adamas, adamantis, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas, “invincible, untamed; hard substance”). Compare Italian diamante.

giavo.etymology: Likely borrowed from Serbo-Croatian đavo/ђаво, from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

bulpo.etymology: Inherited from Latin vulpēs, vulpem. Compare Dalmatian bualp, Venetan bolp, volp, bolpe, Friulian bolp, Ladin volp, Romansh vulp, Italian volpe.

boûz.etymology: From Latin vōcem, accusative singular of vōx. Compare Italian voce, Dalmatian baud, Venetan vóxe, Friulian vôs, Romansh vusch, Romanian boace, Sicilian buci.

guiera.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin werra, borrowed from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”).

batalgia.etymology: Borrowed from Italian battaglia, from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia, from Latin battuō.

glosses_en: Turkey (a country located in Eastern Thrace in Southeastern Europe and Anatolia in West Asia)

truvà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tropāre, from Classical Latin tropus (“song”). Compare Italian trovare, Sicilian truvari.

talgià.etymology: From Late Latin tāliāre, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”). Compare Dalmatian taljur, Venetan tajar.

curtielo.etymology: From Latin cultellus. Compare Dalmatian cortial, Venetan cortèƚo, Italian coltello, cf. also Aromanian curtelã.

veîso.etymology: Ultimately from Latin visus. Compare Italian viso.

uocio.etymology: From Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus. Compare Dalmatian uaclo, Venetan ocio, Italian occhio, Neapolitan uocchio.

pirsigheîn.etymology: Diminutive form ultimately derived from Latin persica, persicum.

manduleîna.etymology: From a diminutive of Vulgar Latin *amandula, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē). Compare Italian mandorla, Friulian mandule.

veisto.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *visitus, from Latin visus. Compare Italian visto.

poûpa.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *puppa, from Latin puppis. Compare Italian poppa.

prùa.etymology: From Latin prōra, from Ancient Greek πρῷρα (prōîra). Compare Italian prua.

drento.etymology: From Latin de + intro. Compare Venetan drénto, Dalmatian drante, Italian dentro.

armileîna.etymology: From Latin armeniacum, from Armenia (“Armenia”). Compare Venetan armelin.

cunprà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”). Compare Venetan conprar, Italian comprare.

fassulito.etymology: Diminutive derived from Vulgar Latin *faciolum, from Latin facies (“face”). Compare Italian fazzoletto, Venetan fasołeto, Friulian façolet, Romansh fazielet, fazalet, Sicilian fazzulettu.

tunduleîno.etymology: From a diminutive derivative of Latin rotundus. Compare Italian tondeggiante, from tondo.

pruoprio.etymology: Ultimately from Latin proprius. Compare Italian proprio.

bucheîn.etymology: Diminutive of buca, from Latin bucca.

uosso.etymology: From Latin ossum, popular variant of os. Compare Dalmatian vuas, Venetan oso, Italian osso, Friulian vues, Romansh ies, oss.

bampa.etymology: Borrowed from Venetan banpa (“blaze, flame”), from Italian vampo (“flame”).

guton.etymology: Ultimately from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun); see cotton for more. Compare Italian cotone, Venetan coton.

bói.etymology: Inherited from Latin bullīre (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (“bubble”).

varguogna.etymology: From Latin verēcundia. Compare Venetan vargogna, Italian vergogna.

pascadur.etymology: From pascà or from Latin piscātor.

favalà.etymology: From Late Latin fābellārī, a verb based on Latin fābella, the diminutive of fābula (“narrative; story”).

tenpesta.etymology: From Latin tempesta, tempestās. Compare Venetan tenpesta, Friulian tampieste.

ruzàda.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *rōsāta, derived from Latin rōs. Compare Italian rugiada.

lavurà.etymology: From Latin labōrāre. Compare Italian lavorare.

rilojo.etymology: From Latin hōrologium, from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion). Compare Venetan rełogio, Italian orologio.

piassa.etymology: From Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa). Compare Italian piazza.

tridase.etymology: From Latin trēdecim. Compare Italian tredici, Venetan tredese, trédexe.

ningun.etymology: From Late Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”).

sareza.etymology: From Vulgar Latin ceresia (possibly through Venetan saréxa), from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of

damognio.etymology: From Latin daemonium, from Ancient Greek δαιμόνιον (daimónion).

spattà.etymology: From Latin aspectō (“observe, look towards”), or from Latin spectō. Compare Venetan spetar, aspetar, Italian aspettare, spettare, Neapolitan aspettà, Romansh spetgar.

maridà.etymology: From Latin marītāre. Compare Venetan maridar.

suorto.etymology: From Latin sors, sortem. Compare Dalmatian suart, Venetan sòrt, Italian sorte, Romanian soartă, Spanish suerte.

uzai.etymology: Plural derived from Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”). Compare Italian uccelli, Venetan osei.

leîbro.etymology: From Latin liber, librum (“book”). Compare Dalmatian lebro, Italian libro, Venetan łìbro.

leîbaro.etymology: From Latin liber, liberum. Compare Venetan łìbaro, Italian libero.

seîma.etymology: From Latin cyma, from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma). Compare Venetan sima, Dalmatian čama, Italian cima.

glosses_en: masculine singular indefinite article a, an

veîda.etymology: From Latin vītis, vītem. Compare Dalmatian vaita, Venetan vida, Italian vite, Romanian viță.

feîo.etymology: From Latin fīlius. Compare Venetan fiol, Dalmatian felj.

veîta.etymology: From Latin vīta. Compare Dalmatian vaita.

peîe.etymology: From a plural of Latin pes, pedem. Compare Italian piedi.

puopulo.etymology: Borrowed from Italian popolo (or heavily influenced by it), from Latin populus.

dasteîn.etymology: From a derivative of Latin dēstinō. Compare Italian destino.

viecio.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.

vanzeîlio.etymology: From Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion).

sparansa.etymology: From Vulgar Latin spērantia, from Latin spērāns.

uorbo.etymology: From Latin orbus. Compare Dalmatian and Friulian vuarb, Venetan and Italian orbo, Romanian orb.

Eîstria.etymology: From Latin Histria, from the ethnicon of the Illyrian tribe of the Histri who inhabited the region.

racumandà.etymology: Ultimately from Latin re- + commandō, commendō. Compare Italian raccomandare.

parparà.etymology: From Latin praeparāre (“to make ready in advance”).

carisa.etymology: From caro. Cognate Italian carezza, Venetan carésa.

deimàn.etymology: From Late Latin dē māne (“early in the morning”). Compare Venetan doman.

scuio.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *scoculum, from Latin scopulus, from Ancient Greek.

muier.etymology: From Latin mulierem. Compare Venetan mojer, Friulian muîr, Dalmatian mojer.

miezanuotto.etymology: Corresponds to Latin mediam noctem. Compare Italian mezzanotte, Romanian miazănoapte.

viseîn.etymology: From Latin vīcīnus. Compare Venetan vesin, Dalmatian vičain, Italian vicino.

mareî.etymology: From Latin marītus. Compare Dalmatian marait, Venetan marìo.

gnagna.etymology: Compare Venetan gnagna, Friulian agne, gnagne.

vesteîti.etymology: Ultimately from Latin vestītus. Compare Italian vestiti.

insembro.etymology: Ultimately from Latin insimul, possibly through Venetan insembre. Compare Italian insieme, French ensemble.

cumio.etymology: From Latin cubitum. Compare Venetan gùmio, comio, Italian gomito.

viduva.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *viduva, from Latin vidua.

furmeîga.etymology: From Latin formīca. Compare Dalmatian formaica, Venetan formìga.

savì.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Latin sapere (“taste, know”).

dulfeîn.etymology: From Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís).

uleîo.etymology: From Latin olīvum, compare olīva. Compare Italian olivo, ulivo.

glosses_en: a little, a while, a short time
puoco.etymology: From Latin paucus. Compare Venetan puòco, Italian poco.

dreîo.etymology: From Late Latin dē retrō. Compare Venetan drio, Italian dietro.

preîmo.etymology: From Latin prīmus. Compare Italian primo, Dalmatian prein.

Ruveîgno.etymology: Ultimately from Latin Arupinum (later Ruvinium, Ruginium, also Mons Rubineus); compare Italian Rovigno, Serbo-Croatian Rovinj.

ganba.etymology: From Late Latin gamba (“hoof”). Compare Venetan ganba, Italian gamba.

screîto.etymology: From Latin scrīptus. Compare Italian scritto.

glosses_en: citizen of the same town or city as another
little creature, animal, beast (e.g. an insect)
bis'ciuleîna.etymology: From a diminutive derivative of Latin bēstiola, itself a diminutive of bēstia. Compare Italian bestiolina, from bestiola.

fioûme.etymology: Inherited from Latin flūmen. Compare Italian fiume.

gninte.etymology: From Latin nec entem. Compare Venetan gnente, Italian niente.

tuorto.etymology: From Latin tortum, substantive use of tortus, perfect passive participle of torqueō. Compare Italian and Venetan torto, Friulian tuart, French tort.

deî.etymology: From Latin dīcit, third-person singular present active indicative of dīcō. Compare Italian dice, Venetan de, Ladin dij.

fadeîga.etymology: From a derivative of Latin fatīgō. Compare Venetan fadiga, Dalmatian fataica, Italian fatica.

lagrama.etymology: From Latin lacrima. Compare Venetan łàgrema, Italian lacrima.

uoca.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *avica, from Classical Latin avis (“bird”). Compare Italian and Venetan oca, Dalmatian jauca, Friulian ocje, Romansh oca, ocha, auca, Sicilian oca, Occitan auca, Catalan oca, French oie.

soûbito.etymology: From Latin subitō, subitus. Compare Italian subito.

stuoria.etymology: Borrowed from Latin historia or Italian storia, either way ultimately from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía).

quisto.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum + iste. Compare Italian questo, Venetan cuesto, Sicilian chistu.

cussèi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum sīc. Compare Dalmatian coisa, Italian così, Venetan cusì.

strento.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *strinctus, from Latin strictus. Compare Venetan strento, old Italian and Neapolitan strinto, Friulian and Ladin strent, Romanian strâmt.

feîn.etymology: From Latin fīnis. Compare Dalmatian fain, Venetan fin, Italian fine.

glosses_en: Luria Lurida, a certain sea snail species
canpaneîl.etymology:
Ultimately derived from Late Latin campāna.
Cognate with Venetan canpanil, canpaniłe, Friulian cjampanîli, cjampanîl, Spanish campanil.

pansà.etymology: From Latin pēnsāre. Doublet of pazà. Compare Italian pensare.

pumoingranà.etymology: From Medieval Latin pomum granatum, from Latin pomum (“fruit”) + granātum (“having many seeds”). Compare Venetan pomoingranà, Old French pomme grenate, compare also Italian melograno, melogranato.

gruota.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *grupta or *crupta, from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ), feminine form of the adjective κρυπτός (kruptós). Compare Italian grotta, Venetan grota.

insignà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin insignāre, from Latin signō.

bucun.etymology: From bóca, from Latin bucca. Compare Venetan bocon, Italian boccone, Sicilian vuccuni.

lanpo.etymology: Ultimately derived from Latin lampas. Compare Venetan lanpo, Italian lampo.

nenbo.etymology: Inherited from Latin nimbus. Compare Venetan nenbo, Italian nembo.

marenda.etymology: From Latin merenda. Compare Ladin marënda, Venetan marenda, Dalmatian marianda, Italian merenda.

fassada.etymology: Ultimately derived from Latin faciēs. Compare Venetan fasada, façada, Italian facciata.

Punente.etymology: From Latin pōnēns, pōnentem. Compare Italian ponente, Sicilian punenti, Spanish poniente, Portuguese poente.

Livante.etymology: From Latin levāns, levāntem. Compare Italian levante.

turnà.etymology: From Latin tornāre (“to turn”). Compare Italian tornare, Venetan tornar, Friulian tornâ, Sicilian turnari, Romansh turnar.

feîsso.etymology: From Latin fixus. Compare Italian fisso.

calsa.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”). Compare Venetan calsa, calça.

scoltà.etymology: Inherited from Latin ascultāre, variant of auscultāre.

reîga.etymology: Ultimately of Germanic origin. Compare Venetan and Italian riga.

scaleîn.etymology: Ultimately derived from Latin scala. Compare Italian scalino, Venetan scalin, scałin.

samèri.etymology: Plural derived ultimately from Late Latin sagmarius, cf. Latin sagma. Compare Dalmatian samur, Italian somarello, somarelli, somaro, somari, Sicilian sumeri, sumaru, Corsican sameri, Old French somier.

foûlmini.etymology: Plural derived from Latin fulmen, fulminis.

suldeîni.etymology: Plural formed from a diminutive of Latin soldus, from solidus. Compare Italian soldino, soldini.

bagnà.etymology: From Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum. Compare Venetan bagnar, Italian bagnare.

infasà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *infasciāre or from Istriot in + Late Latin fasciō, fasciāre, ultimately from Latin fascia. Compare Venetan infasar, Friulian infassâ, Romanian înfășa, Italian fasciare.

vultà.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vol(vi)tāre, derived from Latin volvere.

pitruolgio.etymology: From Medieval Latin petroleum, from Latin petra + oleum. Compare Italian petrolio, Venetan petrojo, Sicilian pitroliu.

deîto.etymology: From Latin dictus. Compare Italian detto.

lìgna.etymology: From Latin ligna, plural of lignum.

bùa.etymology: Borrowed from Venetan boa or Slovene bubati, ultimately of childish origin.

glosses_en: to dine, have dinner, have supper
senà.etymology: From Latin cēnāre, or from Venetan senar.

carpano.etymology: From Latin carpinus. Cf. also Venetan càrpano, Italian carpino.

càvara.etymology: From Latin capra. Compare Venetan càvara, cavra.

uspadal.etymology: From Late Latin hospitālis, hospitāle (“shelter, hospice, guesthouse”), from Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”).

furmajo.etymology: Ultimately from Medieval Latin fōrmāticum, from Latin fōrma (“mould”). May have arrived via Venetan and possibly other intermediaries; cf. Lombard formai.

pagura.etymology: From Latin pavor, pavorem, with a change in suffix, or through a Vulgar Latin root *pavura. Compare Italian paura.

glosses_en: coarse gravel, which gets beaten to small pieces by a hammer
current, which if it hits the coast, goes into two V-branches

cuorno.etymology: From Latin cornū. Compare Dalmatian cuarno.

cuorpo.etymology: From Latin corpus. Compare Italian and Venetan corpo, Dalmatian and Friulian cuarp.

acordà.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accordāre, derived from Latin cor (“heart”).

aradura.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin arātūra, from Latin arō.

bacàn.etymology: Possibly from Latin Bacchānālia (“feast of Bacchus”), from Bacchus (“god of wine”). Compare Italian baccano, French boucan.

glosses_en: to peck, to prick, to feel itchy

arno.etymology: Inherited from Latin antrum (“cave”), from Ancient Greek ἄντρον (ántron).

glosses_en: to be enough, to be sufficient
bastà.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastāre (“to be enough”).

alora.etymology: Inherited from Latin ad illam hōram (literally “at that hour”).

baià.etymology:
Onomatopoeic. Cognate with
Dalmatian bajur, French aboyer, Italian abbaiare, Lombard baià.

bòcia.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bokkia, *buttia (“round object”), from Byzantine Greek βούττια (boúttia), from Ancient Greek βοῦττις (boûttis).

fiùr.etymology: Inherited from Latin flōrem. Compare Venetan fior.

rùia.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rugia, from Latin arrugia (“shaft, pit in goldmine”).

albèo.etymology:
From Latin abiēs (“silver fir”), with the influence of Latin albus (“white”).
Cognate with Venetan albèo, Istriot àlbio.

barìl.etymology: Probably from Old French baril, in turn most likely derived from Proto-Germanic *barilaz.

aguai.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *guai, from Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹 (wai, “woe!”), from Proto-Germanic *wai.

glosses_en: to throw, to toss, to fling
butà.etymology: Either from Old French bouter (“to strike”) or from Gothic *𐌱𐌰𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (*bautan, “to beat”). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bautaną.

abà.etymology: Ultimately from Late Latin abbātem, related with abàte.

abrasà.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adbracchiāre, from Latin ad- + bracchium + -o.

baratà.etymology: Borrowed from Italian barattare, from Old French barater.

budel.etymology: Inherited from Latin botellus, diminutive of botulus (“sausage”).

abadà.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin batāre (“to gape”). Compare Italian abbadare, Romagnol abadêr.

abasìa.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbātia.

abàte.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin abbātem, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”).

abàti.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere.

glosses_en: to form a physical or moral habit
someone who is used to something
abituà.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin habituāre, from Latin habitus.

abordì.etymology: Inherited from Latin abortāre (“to bring forth prematurely”)

acòrsise.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accorrigere, from Latin ad- + corrigō (“to correct”).

adàto.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin adaptus, from ad- + aptus (“suitable”).

afanàse.etymology: Uncertain. Cognate with Italian affannare (“to leave breathless”).

agrùn.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *agrum, ācrus, from Latin ācer, from Proto-Italic *akris, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós (“sharp”).

agurà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *agurāre, from Latin augurāre.

àier.etymology: Inherited from Latin āērea or āēre, from āēr.

glosses_en: madia, a wooden bowl for kneading bread
alból.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *albeus (“kneading trough”), from Latin alveus. Cognate with Venetan albol.

alcoliſa.etymology: From Medieval Latin alcohol, ultimately from Arabic اَلْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”).

àle.etymology: Borrowed from French allez, from Early Medieval Latin alāre.

glosses_en: a tree of the genus cuscuta

alevà.etymology: From Latin allevāre (“to lift up, alleviate”).

alméno.etymology: From al + méno. Cognate with Italian almeno.

alonſi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longe.

glosses_en: sessitura, a fold sewn by hand at the bottom of a garment, to extend or to shorten it

altésa.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin altitia, from Latin altus (“high”).

àmolo.etymology: Unknown. Possibly of Gaulish origin. Cognate with Italian amolo, Venetan àmoło.

anàda.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *annāta, from Latin annāre.

ananti.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin ab ante.

bòta.etymology: From the verb bottare, probably derived from Old French boter (“to strike”), from Frankish *buttan, from Frankish *bautan (“to hit, strike”).

anbòl.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *albeus, from Latin alvear or alvearium.

ancòi.etymology:
Inherited from Latin hinc hodie.
Cognate with Lombard incoeu, Venetan ancoi, Emilian incû, Piedmontese ancheuj, Ligurian ancheu, Ladin incö.

ancóra.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hāncora, from Latin in hanc horām (“until this hour”).

ancùſeno.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incūdinem, possibly via Italian ancugine or Venetan ancùxene, ultimately from Latin incus.

andròna.etymology: Inherited from Latin andron, from Ancient Greek ἀνδρών (andrṓn).

ànera.etymology: From an older form *ànedra (with later assimilation of /dr/ to /rr/), derived from Vulgar Latin *anatria, from Latin anatem. Compare Italian anatra, Dalmatian ànera, Venetan ànara and others.

angunìa.etymology: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin agōnia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía).

anguſèl.etymology: Ultimately from Latin acus. Cognate with Venetan angusiola.

ansà.etymology: From Late Latin anxiāre (“to make uneasy or anxious”).

glosses_en: a female given name, equivalent to English Angela
a male given name, equivalent to English Angelo

ansiprèso.etymology:
Compare Italian noce pesca, pesca noce (“nectarine”), Venetan naspèrgeso (“nectarine”), Maltese nuċiprisk (“nectarine”), Sicilian nucipèrsicu (“cypress”) for similar developments.
Ultimately from Late Latin cypressus.

glosses_en: a female given name, equivalent to English Antonia
The opening of the year, spring

aquavita.etymology: Calque of Medieval Latin aqua vitae (literally “water of life”).

briva.etymology: From brivar, abrivar, from Old Occitan abrivar.

arénto.etymology: Either from Latin adhaerēre or from Latin ad rādentem.

glosses_en: a mill tool, like a presser

àrgheno.etymology: Inherited from Latin organum (“instrument, implement, tool”).

arménta.etymology: Inherited from Latin armentum, from Latin armenta, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-mn̥-teh₂, from *h₂er- (“to join”) + *-mn̥ + *-teh₂.

armogno.etymology: Inherited from Latin organum. See Asturian muérganu for similar developments.

arpìſ.etymology: From Venetan [Term?], ultimately from Ancient Greek ἅρπαξ (hárpax, “grappling-iron; flesh-hook”). Cognate with Italian arpese.

glosses_en: to barricade or frame an object to an iron wire

arsìſ.etymology: From Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).

asàl.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin aciārium, derived from Latin aciēs (“sharp point”).

àſera.etymology: Possibly from Latin aggerem (“rubble; mound; rampart”).

aſguélto.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *exvellere, from Latin vellere (“to pluck, stretch”).

asìl.etymology: From Latin assis, variant of axis.

astigà.etymology: Uncertain. Either from Latin oscillārī, perhaps from Vulgar Latin *osllicāre, or from Vulgar Latin *exquatere, *excotere, ultimately from Latin quatere (“shake, agitiate”).

astiòſ.etymology: Similar development like Italian astioso. From astio.

aténdi.etymology: From Latin attendere, adtendere (“to pay attention to, attend”).

atrèso.etymology: Inherited from Latin attractum. Cognate with Italian attrezzo.

babàu.etymology: Onomatopoeic, imitating dogs. Cognate with Italian babau, Old French baboe, Romanian baubau.

bacalà.etymology: From Dutch bakkeljauw, of uncertain origin. Compare Italian baccalà, Sicilian baccalaru, Catalan bacallà, Spanish bacalao, Portuguese bacalhau.

bacìsa.etymology: Unknown, there could be some connection to batì.

bàcolo.etymology: Uncertain. Either derived from Vulgar Latin *blattula, from Latin blatta or from Venetan bao with added suffix -acolo.

badìl.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bātile, from Latin batillum.

bagatìn.etymology: A small copper coin used in the medieval ages, from Italian bagattino, bagatino, of uncertain origin. Compare Italian bagattella.

bagolà.etymology: From Venetan bigoli (“spaghetti; (dialectal slang) euphemism for body part”).

bàla.etymology:
Uncertain.
Either:
* From Medieval Latin balla, from Frankish *ballu
* From Lombardic *palla.
Ultimately both derive from Proto-Germanic *ballô, *balluz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blow, swell, inflate”).

bampàda.etymology: From Italian vampata, likely via Venetan.

barafuſa.etymology: Unknown. It has been suggested to be a compound of baraònda and confusion, biroufan and confusion, or of onomatopoeic origin.

barbabiétola.etymology: Inherited from Latin herba bēta with influence from barba.

barbastél.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vespertillum (reshaped with analogy with other nouns).

glosses_en: shoot or cutting of a vine
barbatèla.etymology: From barba. Cognate with Italian barbatella.

glosses_en: to babble, in the infant stage
barbustà.etymology: Inherited from Latin balbūtīre, from Latin balbus (“stammering”).

barcón.etymology: Of Germanic origin; possibly from Lombardic balko (“beam”), from Proto-Germanic *balkô (“beam”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“beam, pile, prop”). Compare Friulian balcon and Venetan balcon.

barè.etymology: Probably from Proto-Celtic *barros. Cognate with Welsh bar and Irish barr.

glosses_en: the doffing of one's cap to greet someone

barufa.etymology:
Two possibilities:
* Either onomatopoeic
* Or derived from a Proto-Germanic *raup-. If so, cognate with Old Norse raup, Icelandic raup.

glosses_en: a kiss on a hand to show respect
basil, a herb of species Ocimum basilicum
baſigol.etymology: Inherited from Latin basilicum, from Ancient Greek βασιλικόν (basilikón), nominalized neuter form of the adjective βασιλικός (basilikós, “royal, kingly”), derived from βασιλεύς (basileús, “master; king”).

glosses_en: the base which the millstone rests
baſìl.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bacchinon, probably of Gaulish origin.

glosses_en: to go mad, to go insane
basilà.etymology: Borrowed from Italian vacillare, from Latin vacillāre.

baſilisco.etymology: Borrowed from Latin basiliscus, from Ancient Greek βασιλίσκος (basilískos, “little king”), diminutive of βασιλεύς (basileús, “chief, king”).

bastìn.etymology: Inherited from Latin bastum, from Vulgar Latin *bastō.

glosses_en: small boat, typical of Rovinj fishermen
batana.etymology: Derived from Old English bāt, sharing the same root as batièl.

batibùio.etymology:
From bati + bùio.
The second compound either derives from Latin bullīre (“to boil”), or is cognate with Italian bugliare (“to mutiny, to rise up”).

batiſà.etymology: Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin baptidiō, from Late Latin baptizō, from Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to plunge”).

glosses_en: traditional ceremony after mass on Good Friday, where churchgoers invoked the Passion of Christ by beating the pews with a wooden object

batòcio.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *battuaculum, derived from Latin battō. The sense of fool probably relates to children's ridicule.

glosses_en: wooden instrument used as replacement of bells during Holy Week
bàtola.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *battulum (“wood blade”), from Latin battō. Cognate with Venetan batola.

baùl.etymology: Borrowed from Spanish baúl. From French bahut. Further origin uncertain.

becasòco.etymology: Compound of beca + sòco (“crow”). The first term comes from a Proto-Celtic root *bacc-. The second term comes from Latin cornīcula.

belagànba.etymology: Probably a compound of biel (“beautiful”) + ganba (“leg”).

belànsa.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin *bilancia, from Latin bilanx, from bi- and lanx.

besàca.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bisacca, from Late Latin bisaccium.

bevànda.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bibanda, from Latin bibenda.

glosses_en: to coat with a layer of paint

biastemà.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin blastēmāre, from Latin blasphēmō, from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω (blasphēméō).

biàva.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin bladum, with the /v/ being added to avoid /aa/.

bibilùsegno.etymology: Similar to bibieso (“slow, hard tiring work”).

bièco.etymology: Possibly from Slovene, from German Fleck.

bìgolo.etymology: From the same root as bicato.

bigòto.etymology: Borrowed from French bigot, possibly from Old High German bī got, see further at English bigot.

bilfo.etymology: The most probable origin of this word is a borrowing of Middle High German bilwiz, which has an uncertain origin.

bìo.etymology: Inherited from Latin bombȳcum, via apheresis. Compare Italian baco.

glosses_en: to hop as cattle due to horseflies
biolà.etymology: Ive suggests an origin in bìo, but the explanation is not convincing. Rather from bigulà.

glosses_en: to get by in a situation
to plunge, to sink, to submerge

biſàsa.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bisaccia. Doublet of besàca.

biſàto.etymology: Uncertain, probably from Vulgar Latin *bīstia, from Latin bēstia. Cognate with Italian biso.

biscotà.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin biscoctum.

bisìga.etymology: Inherited from Latin vessīca, from Latin vēsīca.

bisìn.etymology: Diminutive of bis, of onomatopoeic origin.

glosses_en: a dice made out of bones to play games

boèr.etymology: Inherited from Latin bovārius or boārius, from Latin bōs.

bombàſ.etymology: Inherited from Medieval Latin bombacium, from Byzantine Greek βαμβάκιον (bambákion), from either Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax, “cotton”) or Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux, “silk-worm”), whose ultimate origin is unknown, possibly related to Mi

bonagrasia.etymology: Borrowed from French bonne grâce. The term developed as it was inviting for the tailors. Later on, clothes were hung along a small board inside the rod.

glosses_en: to set, to go down, to sink

bonbaſìna.etymology: Borrowed from Venetan bonbaso (“thick cloth”). Compare French bombasin.

boracia.etymology: Borrowed from Venetan borachia, from Spanish borracha.

glosses_en: tightly-coiled cloth pad placed on the head to support loads

bòsolo.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin baucia. Cognate with Spanish bocho.

glosses_en: small bottle for wine and water
botàso.etymology: Cognate with buto. Possibly derived from bottaccio. Ultimately from Late Latin buttis.

bòto.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin buttis, probably of Ancient Greek origin.

bóto.etymology: From Old Istriot bottare which dates back to an onomatopoeic bott (“to blow”).

glosses_en: to grasp, to clasp, to clutch

bràvo.etymology: Uncertain, probably from Vulgar Latin *bravus, from a fusion of Latin prāvus and barbarus. See Italian bravo for more.

glosses_en: arms around neck, to hug someone warmly
to cradle in one's arms, to swing gently

braſòla.etymology: One hypothesis claims that it comes from Proto-Germanic *brasen (“to roast”). But compare Italian braciola, from Gothic *𐌱𐍂𐌰𐍃𐌰 (*brasa), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰres- (“to crack, break, burst”).

glosses_en: wooden collar that encircles the ox's neck from the lower part
reaction after making a mistake in a game or something else

brèna.etymology: Perhaps Borrowed from Old French bride, in turn from Middle High German brīdel (“rein, bridle”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *brigdil (“bridle”).

glosses_en: small hail in the summer with irregular, broken grains
wooden tub for collecting grapes and later pressing them

brìscola.etymology: Perhaps borrowed from French brisque, of unknown origin. Compare Italian briscola, Serbo-Croatian briškula, Portuguese bisca.

briſina.etymology: Blend of Latin pruīna (“hoarfrost”) + German Brise (“breeze”).

brìtola.etymology:
There are many suggestions for the etymology for this word:
* Borrowed from French brette, bretailler.
* From Proto-Celtic, cognate with Old Irish berraid.
* From Brittian.
* Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian britva (“razor”).

bròcolo.etymology: From Latin broccus, of Gaulish origin.

glosses_en: a fish stew, similar to bouillabaisse
brodeto.etymology: From Medieval Latin brudettus, from Medieval Latin brodium.

bronſo.etymology: Uncertain. There are many proposals given for its origin (see Italian bronzo). It is first attested in northern Italy and spread south. Pellizzer agrees the most with a source in birinǧ (“bronze, brass”) or a dialectical variant *b(u)runǧ.

brontolà.etymology: From Ancient Greek βροντή (brontḗ, “thunder”), of onomatopoeic origin.

broſa.etymology: From Middle High German broz (“sprout”), from Proto-Germanic *brutą.

brunél.etymology: From brunello, borrowed from French prunelle.

glosses_en: to cut branches off a tree after it has been felled.
bruscà.etymology: From bruscare (“to remove old pitch and leave it to dry on a ship”), or from brùsco (“twig”).

bruschèra.etymology: Inherited from Latin ruscus with influence from Gaulish *bruscus.

bruschìn.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin *bruscia, itself from Latin brūscum (“knot, excrescence on a tree”) or Proto-Germanic *bruskaz (“underbush”) or a confluence of these.

glosses_en: small scrap of wood left by cutting wood with an axe used to start a fire
herb grown in the fields and used to season cooked snails

brustolà.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *brustulāre, from a blend of Latin brusiare and ustulāre.

buàsa.etymology: From a Celtic substrate language, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷew- (“excrement; dung”) or Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (“cow”). Cognate with French bouse, Piedmontese busa, Ligurian bêusa, bûsa, bûsia, Occitan bosa, bosia and Veneta

glosses_en: a big, non-poisonous snake frequenting the area in hot periods
buasèra.etymology: Inherited from Latin boa. Doublet of boa.

bucàl.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin baucālis, from Koine Greek βαύκαλις (baúkalis, “container used for the cooling of wine”), of Berber or Egyptian origin.

glosses_en: cloth used to cover the laundry when pouring ash on it

bugàda.etymology: Borrowed from Venetan bugada, from Vulgar Latin *būcāta, from Frankish *būkōn (“to soak, wash”).

buligà.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bullicāre (“boil”), from Latin bulliō (“bubble”).

glosses_en: to set, to go down, to sink (of the sun, moon or stars)

buratà.etymology: From Medieval Latin *būra, from Middle High German biuteln, biūtel from Old High German butil (“pouch, bag”), from Proto-West Germanic *būdil (“pouch, bag”).

buréla.etymology: Borrowed from Old Italian borro (“cork, round object”).

buriòn.etymology: Either a word related to Latin boreās (“north wind”), or borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بوراغان (burağan, “whirlwind, tornado”).

glosses_en: small amount of wine produced in september before the grapes ripen
burìsolo.etymology: Possibly from buràcia (“canteen”), from Spanish borracha (“wineskin”).

buſ.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin būca, a variant of Latin bucca (“mouth”).

glosses_en: type of olive grown in the Istria region
to swindle, to cheat, to deceive
buſarà.etymology: Borrowed from Venetan busarare, buzarare, from Medieval Latin Bulgari (“Bulgarian”), from Old Church Slavonic блъгаринъ (blŭgarinŭ), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bulgar (“disturber”). Compare Italian buggerare.

buſia.etymology: From Old Occitan bauzia, from Frankish *bausī (“evil, wicked”) (or via Vulgar Latin *bauscia), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bausuz.

butada.etymology: From either butà or directly from Old French bouter (“to blow, to strike”).

àbaco.etymology: Borrowed from Latin abacus (“counting board”), from Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax, “board”).
